# Solar Power along the Sun Belt (2015-2024)

This project was an independent endeavor in order to determine the growth of solar power over time in four major states along the Sun Belt: California, Arizona, Texas, and Florida. These states rank top four in the United States solar industry.

This project aimed to examine how the different contexts of each state (size, policy, or location) impact the growth of the solar industry over the past decade.

I pulled data from a public API within the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) from 2015 until 2024. Using Python to clean and filter the data with pandas, I created a plot-by-plot comparison of the four states. I chose to separate the four states rather than keep them in the same plot because of California's overwhelming advantage over the others in terms of Megawatt-hours generation. This is likely due to the sunshine received and climate policies in place. I also created a table comparing each states slope and compound annual growth rate.


```python
import os
import requests  # type: ignore
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from dotenv import load_dotenv  # type: ignore

load_dotenv()

API_KEY = os.environ.get("EIA_API_KEY")

if not API_KEY:
    raise ValueError("EIA_API_KEY environment variable not set. See README for setup.")

# EIA's Electricty Generation Data
url = "https://api.eia.gov/v2/electricity/electric-power-operational-data/data/"

# Comparing states in the U.S. Sun Belt region
states = ["FL", "TX", "CA", "AZ"]
state_names = {"FL": "Florida", "TX": "Texas", "CA": "California", "AZ": "Arizona"}
colors = {"FL": "#319941", "TX": "#D0D76D", "CA": "#1C618F", "AZ": "#E168C3"}

all_states = []

# Filtering by solar generation, annual data, and the Sun Belt States
for state in states:
    params = {
        "api_key": API_KEY,
        "frequency": "annual",         
        "data[0]": "generation",
        "facets[fueltypeid][]": "SUN",
        "facets[location][]": state,
        "start": "2015",
        "end": "2024",
        "sort[0][column]": "period",
        "sort[0][direction]": "asc",
        "length": "500",
    }

    response = requests.get(url, params=params)

    if response.status_code != 200:
        print(f"Failed to fetch {state}: {response.status_code}")
        print(response.text)
        continue

    raw = response.json()
    data = raw["response"]["data"]
    state_df = pd.DataFrame(data)
    state_df = state_df[state_df["sectorid"] == "99"]
    all_states.append(state_df)
    print(f"Fetched {state} successfully")

solar_gen = pd.concat(all_states, ignore_index=True)

# Cleaning!
solar_gen = solar_gen.rename(columns={
    "period": "year",
    "generation": "generation_mwh",
    "location": "state"
})

# Converting the year and generation (in megawatt-hours) to numeric
solar_gen["year"] = pd.to_numeric(solar_gen["year"])
solar_gen["generation_mwh"] = pd.to_numeric(solar_gen["generation_mwh"])

# Grouping by year and state
solar_gen = solar_gen.groupby(["year", "state"], as_index=False)["generation_mwh"].sum()
solar_gen["generation_twh"] = solar_gen["generation_mwh"] / 1000

# Four subplots because of scale differences
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 8), sharex=True)
axes = axes.flatten()  

for ax, state in zip(axes, states):
    state_data = solar_gen[solar_gen["state"] == state]
    ax.bar(
        state_data["year"],
        state_data["generation_twh"],
        color=colors[state],
        edgecolor="white",
        linewidth=0.5
    )
    ax.plot(
        state_data["year"],
        state_data["generation_twh"],
        color="#000000",
        linewidth=1.5,
        marker="o",
        markersize=4
    )
    ax.set_title(state_names[state], fontsize=13, fontweight="bold")
    ax.set_ylabel("Generation (TWh)", fontsize=10)
    ax.spines["top"].set_visible(False)
    ax.spines["right"].set_visible(False)
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=45)

fig.suptitle(
    "Sun Belt Solar Energy Generation by State (2015–2024)",
    fontsize=16,
    fontweight="bold"
)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Save combined dataset for reuse
solar_gen[["year", "state", "generation_twh"]].to_csv("sunbelt_solar_data.csv", index=False)
```
### Findings

California led all four states in electricity generation, reaching up to 50 terawatt-hours (TWh) by 2024. Texas was a close second with 40 TWh. From the graph, it appears that Texas and Florida had the largest leaps in growth, while Arizona has had the slowest growth.

```python
import numpy as np

results = []

for state in states:
    state_data = solar_gen[solar_gen["state"] == state].sort_values("year")
    
    years = state_data["year"].values
    values = state_data["generation_twh"].values

    slope, intercept = np.polyfit(years, values, 1)

    # Percent growth from first year to last year
    start_val = values[0]
    end_val = values[-1]
    pct_growth = ((end_val - start_val) / start_val) * 100
    
    # CAGR - compound annual growth rate metrics to see which state grew the fastest
    num_years = years[-1] - years[0]
    cagr = ((end_val / start_val) ** (1 / num_years) - 1) * 100
    
    results.append({
        "state": state_names[state],
        "slope_twh_per_year": round(slope, 3),
        "pct_growth": round(pct_growth, 1),
        "cagr_pct": round(cagr, 1)
    })

growth_df = pd.DataFrame(results)
growth_df = growth_df.sort_values("cagr_pct", ascending=False)
print(growth_df)
```

```{r growth-table, echo = F}
library(knitr)
growth <- read.csv("C:/Users/wplov/Python/sunbelt_solar_growth.csv")
kable(growth,
      col.names = c("State", "Slope (TWh/yr)", "% Growth (2015–2024)", "CAGR (%)"),
      align = "c")
```
Here, we can see that Texas had the greatest growth relative to its starting point in solar power generation from 2015 to 2024, with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 67%. While California leads the four states in solar generation quantities, Texas has experienced the most growth. This is relevant to the future of solar in the United States. With similar policies to California's current clean-energy mandates, Texas could surpass California in solar generation.
